messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] "slm" model using rgeneric
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] "slm" model using rgeneric
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The slm model has already been implemented in INLA:

https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7390/9/17/2044

https://www.mdpi.com/2225-1146/8/2/23

In the first paper you will find details about the implementation. In your implementation (I checked it very quickly) I believe that the graph definition is wrong as it should have non-zero entries in the places where the precision matrix is non-zero. Also, some of these models have been implemented using the generic0 latent effect:

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211675314000037

Finally, please check the documentation of the slmlaten effect in INLA: inla.doc(“slm”)

Best,

Virgilio

The fact is that I want to extend these spatial lag models.

I have a presumptuous request I wonder if you can give a similar implementation of "slm" using rgeneric?

Best wishes
Charles

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Online learning with INLA
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Online learning with INLA
messages.body_plain:
The issue about online learning is that the Markov properties of the
latent is lost with marginalisation. the marginal for the latent state
at time t, conditioned on all previous time points, is no longer Markov
ie its precision matrix is dense, hence all computational benefits are
lost and you're back to dense matrix formulation and not within the INLA
(computational) framework.

so in a 'online'/dynamic framework where you want to do all the time one
step ahead forecast, and constantly revising the model with new data,
with INLA, then you use a moving window approach.

do t+1 forecast fitting the model from time 1 to t

observe new data y_t+1

do t+2 forecost fitting the model from time 2 to t+1, thus including
y_t+1 but removing y_1

you can use the first fit as an initial value for the second one hence
speeding it up.

this will implcitely gives you a 'model' with time-varying parameters
and hyperparameters, I guess you get my point. the length of the window
is whatever you're confortable with.

there is a way to let the posterior of the hyperparameters be the joint
prior in another inla() call, but that will not work here as there are
overlap of data in the two fits. unless you're willing to assuming some
discounting scheme, which is actually very reasonable here I would guess

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
I'm still having trouble with time-varying covariates with the Cox model. I'm trying to use Model B located here: "https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/r/examples/alda/r-applied-longitudinal-data-analysis-ch-15/

The code give error: "Error in max(sapply(y.surv, length)) : invalid 'type' (list) of argument"

Any help would be greatly appreciated:

------------------------
rm(list=ls())

library(survival)
library(INLA)

## https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/r/examples/alda/r-applied-longitudinal-data-analysis-ch-15/

cocaine <- read.csv("https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/stat/examples/alda/firstcocaine.csv")
cocaine$EVENT <- 1 - cocaine$CENSOR
cocaine <- cocaine[, c("ID", "BIRTHYR", "COKEAGE", "EARLYMJ", "EARLYOD",
                       "EVENT", "MJAGE", "ODAGE", "SELLMJAGE", "SDAGE")]

###############
### Model B ###
###############

longModBDF <- tmerge(
    cocaine,
    cocaine,
    id = ID,
    start_using = event(COKEAGE, EVENT),
    USEMJ = tdc(MJAGE),
    USEOD = tdc(ODAGE)
)
head(longModBDF[order(longModBDF$ID),])

modB <- coxph(Surv(tstart, tstop, start_using) ~ BIRTHYR + USEMJ + USEOD,
              data= longModBDF, ties="efron")
summary(modB)

### INLA ###

y.surv <- inla.surv(
    time=longModBDF$tstop,
    event=longModBDF$start_using,
    truncation=longModBDF$tstart
)

f <- y.surv ~ 1 + BIRTHYR + USEMJ + USEOD
mod.inla.cox <- inla.coxph(
    f,
    data=longModBDF,
    control.hazard=list(n.intervals=30)
)

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: More on Cox model with time-varying covariates
messages.body_plain:
In your example, the time points are equally spaced and there are not so many so yes, you can just set cutpoints for integers between 1 and 42 (i.e., max observed time). When there are many event times, and some of them are very close to each other, it is easier to just set more intervals (just increase the n.interval so you have a fine resolution). An alternative approach is to impute the time-dependent covariate values for the corresponding intervals if you want to keep the cutpoints at specific values but it's more involved and likely less accurate.

Best,
Denis

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] sum-to-zero constraint
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] sum-to-zero constraint
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid' model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long range correlation that interacts with some other model component. You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model component includes its null space.

Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the fact that you do not always need to add a constraint while working with intrinsic models.

library(INLA)

n <- 30
x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))

plot(x)

y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))

fit1 <- inla(
    y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
    data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
    family = 'poisson'
)

## The intercept captures the overall mean
fit1$summary.fix

## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around zero
summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)

## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
fit2 <- inla(
    y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
    data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
    family = 'poisson'
)

## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not fitted separately)
summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)

## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same as the priors are different and there are some small numerical differences while doing the computations)
summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)

regards,
Elias

> > > formula <- O ~ X +   f(ID.area1, X, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > >   f(ID.area2, model="besag", graph=TR.adj, constr=T) +
> > >   f(ID.area3, model="iid", constr=F)

> > >
> > > On Thursday 7 March 2024 at 09:59:30 UTC+3:30 Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hi,
> > > >
> > > > You do not always need constr = TRUE. It is not needed for 'iid' model, or any other model with proper joint distribution. But sometimes you want it, for example for the case of having a long range correlation that interacts with some other model component. You only need constraint in intrinsic models if another model component includes its null space.
> > > >
> > > > Please take a look at the example below, where I illustrate the fact that you do not always need to add a constraint while working with intrinsic models.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > library(INLA)
> > > >
> > > > n <- 30
> > > > x <- scale(cumsum(rnorm(n)))
> > > >
> > > > plot(x)
> > > >
> > > > y <- rpois(n, exp(2 + x))
> > > >
> > > > fit1 <- inla(
> > > >     y ~ f(i, model = 'rw1'),
> > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > )
> > > >
> > > > ## The intercept captures the overall mean
> > > > fit1$summary.fix
> > > >
> > > > ## posterior mean for the constrained random effect is around zero
> > > > summary(fit1$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > >
> > > > ## Now, take the intercept ou of the linear predictor
> > > > ## Then, the constraint in the random effect is no longer needed
> > > > fit2 <- inla(
> > > >     y ~ 0 + f(i, model = 'rw1', constr = FALSE),
> > > >     data = list(i = 1:n, y = y),
> > > >     family = 'poisson'
> > > > )
> > > >
> > > > ## unconstrained random effect is around the intercept (not fitted separately)
> > > > summary(fit2$summary.random$i$mean)
> > > >
> > > > ## However, the fitted values are similar (not exactly the same as the priors are different and there are some small numerical differences while doing the computations)
> > > > summary(fit1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > > summary(fit2$summary.fitted.values$mean)
> > > >
> > > > regards,
> > > > Elias
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, 7 Mar 2024 at 08:34, Reza Hajipour <rehaj...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > >   f(ID.year, model="rw2", constr=TRUE) +

I am trying to model the spatiotemporal distribution of a species by considering size as another dimension.

We expect that the spatial distribution of similar sized individuals is similar, thus, in a purely spatial scenario I could do something like this:

sp_size = 1:10

In INLA:
s_index <- inla.spde.make.index('s', n.spde = spde$n.spde, n.group = max(sp_size ))
f(s, model = spde, group = s.group, control.group = list(model = 'ar1))

in inlabru:
field_S_size(coordinates, model=spde, group =  sp_size   , ngroup = max(sp_size ),control.group = list(model="ar1"))

where I would be linking the spatial distributions of sizes by an AR1 process.

But what if I want to add the temporal dimension through another AR1 process? would this be possible?

Cheers,
iosu

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Analysis of Residuals from ZAP INLA with spatial autocorrelation and DHARMa
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Analysis of Residuals from ZAP INLA with spatial autocorrelation and DHARMa
messages.body_plain:
I am finally getting back to this. Here is some code borrowed from the
inlabru ZAP vignette that incorporates suggestions from Alain and Finn.
This should get you going on using DHARMa for model fit evaluation.
Note that the ZAP vignette also shows alternative ways to evaluate
model fit using PIT histograms or Q-Q plots.

# libraries
library(VGAM)
library(ggplot2)
library(inlabru)
library(terra) # use latest version
library(sf)
library(dplyr)

# grab data and modeling objects
gorillas_sf <- inlabru::gorillas_sf
nests <- gorillas_sf$nests
mesh <- gorillas_sf$mesh
boundary <- gorillas_sf$boundary
gcov <- gorillas_sf_gcov()
counts_rstr <- terra::rasterize(vect(nests), gcov, fun = sum, background = 0) %>%
  terra::aggregate(fact = 4, fun = sum) %>% mask(vect(boundary))
counts_rstr <- counts_rstr %>% cellSize(unit = "km") %>% c(counts_rstr)

# pull counts and covariates
counts_df <- crds(counts_rstr, df = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) %>%
  bind_cols(values(counts_rstr, mat = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  rename(count = sum) %>%
  mutate(present = count > 0) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = st_crs(nests))
gcov_lvls <- gcov$vegetation %>% levels()
gcov_vegetation <- gcov$vegetation %>%
  segregate() %>%
  terra::aggregate(fact = 4, fun = mean)
names(gcov_vegetation) <- gcov_lvls[[1]]$vegetation

# make mesh and spatial model
px_mesh <- fm_mesh_2d_inla(
  loc = st_intersection(st_as_sfc(counts_df), st_buffer(boundary, -0.05)),
  boundary = boundary,
  max.edge = c(0.5, 1),
  crs = st_crs(counts_df))
px_matern <- INLA::inla.spde2.pcmatern(px_mesh,
                                       prior.sigma = c(0.1, 0.01),
                                       prior.range = c(0.1, 0.01))

# define model components and likelihood
comps <- ~ veg_disturbed(gcov_vegetation$Disturbed, model = "linear") +
  veg_grassland(gcov_vegetation$Grassland, model = "linear") +
  elevation(gcov$elevation, model = "linear") +
  field(geometry, model = px_matern) + Intercept_present(1) + Intercept_count(1) +
  elevation_present(gcov$elevation, model = "linear") +
  field_present(geometry, copy = "field")
truncated_poisson_like <-
  if (package_version(getNamespaceVersion("INLA")) < "2023.10.19-1") {
    like(family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
      data = counts_df[counts_df$present, ],
      formula = count ~ elevation + field + Intercept_count,
      E = area,
      control.family = list(hyper = list(theta = list(
        initial = -20, fixed = TRUE))))
  } else {
    like(family = "nzpoisson",
      data = counts_df[counts_df$present, ],
      formula = count ~ elevation + field + Intercept_count,
      E = area)}

# fit zap model
fit_zap <- bru(
  comps,
  like(family = "binomial", data = counts_df,
    formula = present ~ veg_disturbed + veg_grassland +
      elevation_present + field_present + Intercept_present),
  truncated_poisson_like)
summary(fit_zap)

# get simulated count samples
pred_zap <- generate(
  fit_zap, ## this is model
  counts_df, ## these are data for prediction
  ~ {presence_prob <- ## get vector of p per posterior sample
           plogis(veg_disturbed + veg_grassland + elevation_present +
                       field_present + Intercept_present)
        lambda <- exp(elevation + field + Intercept_count) ## get lambdas
        ## simulate integer counts with function from VGAM
        sim <-  VGAM::rzapois(n=length(lambda), lambda=lambda*area,
                          pobs0=1-presence_prob)
    # define output from generate
    list(presence = presence_prob,
      lambda = lambda,
      sim = sim)},
  n.samples = 100)

# extract simulated counts from sample list object
sims <- as.matrix(as.data.frame(t(do.call(rbind,
                                   lapply(pred_zap, function(x) x[["sim"]])))))

# evaluate simulated counts with DHARMa
res <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse=sims,
                    observedResponse=counts_df$count,
                    integerResponse = T)
plot(res)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Yes, if you’re using the dual mesh approach to manually construct an LGCP approximation in plain inla you’re not using the same method as inlabru. Inlabru uses the method from the Going off Grid paper, which (contrary to popular belief) does _not_ use the dual mesh (the plot of the dual mesh in the paper just illustrates the the basis functions have the same integrals as the areas in the dual mesh). The dual mesh approaches in some examples are lower order approximations.
In addition, inlabru by default combines all the log(lambda) terms into a single predictor likelihood contribution, which may affect how DIC is computed.  So you should be able to compare DIC between inla() models, and between bru() models, but not necessarily between inla&bru models unless you implement the inlabru method in inla() yourself.

Another difference, which might be the reason for differences, is that the default prior for the intercept is currently not the same in inla() and bru(). Set it explicitly with Intercept(1, prec.linear=…) to see if that changes things.

Finn

On Tue, 12 Mar 2024 at 21:49, Tim Meehan <tme...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am finally getting back to this. Here is some code borrowed from the
> inlabru ZAP vignette that incorporates suggestions from Alain and Finn.
> This should get you going on using DHARMa for model fit evaluation.
> Note that the ZAP vignette also shows alternative ways to evaluate
> model fit using PIT histograms or Q-Q plots.
>
> # libraries
> library(VGAM)
> library(ggplot2)
> library(inlabru)
> library(terra) # use latest version
> library(sf)
> library(dplyr)
>
> # grab data and modeling objects
> gorillas_sf <- inlabru::gorillas_sf
> nests <- gorillas_sf$nests
> mesh <- gorillas_sf$mesh
> boundary <- gorillas_sf$boundary
> gcov <- gorillas_sf_gcov()
> counts_rstr <- terra::rasterize(vect(nests), gcov, fun = sum, background = 0) %>%
>   terra::aggregate(fact = 4, fun = sum) %>% mask(vect(boundary))
> counts_rstr <- counts_rstr %>% cellSize(unit = "km") %>% c(counts_rstr)
>
> # pull counts and covariates
> counts_df <- crds(counts_rstr, df = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) %>%
>   bind_cols(values(counts_rstr, mat = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
>   rename(count = sum) %>%
>   mutate(present = count > 0) %>%
>   st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = st_crs(nests))
> gcov_lvls <- gcov$vegetation %>% levels()
> gcov_vegetation <- gcov$vegetation %>%
>   segregate() %>%
>   terra::aggregate(fact = 4, fun = mean)
> names(gcov_vegetation) <- gcov_lvls[[1]]$vegetation
>
> # make mesh and spatial model
> px_mesh <- fm_mesh_2d_inla(
>   loc = st_intersection(st_as_sfc(counts_df), st_buffer(boundary, -0.05)),
>   boundary = boundary,
>   max.edge = c(0.5, 1),
>   crs = st_crs(counts_df))
> px_matern <- INLA::inla.spde2.pcmatern(px_mesh,
>                                        prior.sigma = c(0.1, 0.01),
>                                        prior.range = c(0.1, 0.01))
>
> # define model components and likelihood
> comps <- ~ veg_disturbed(gcov_vegetation$Disturbed, model = "linear") +
>   veg_grassland(gcov_vegetation$Grassland, model = "linear") +
>   elevation(gcov$elevation, model = "linear") +
>   field(geometry, model = px_matern) + Intercept_present(1) + Intercept_count(1) +
>   elevation_present(gcov$elevation, model = "linear") +
>   field_present(geometry, copy = "field")
> truncated_poisson_like <-
>   if (package_version(getNamespaceVersion("INLA")) < "2023.10.19-1") {
>     like(family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
>       data = counts_df[counts_df$present, ],
>       formula = count ~ elevation + field + Intercept_count,
>       E = area,
>       control.family = list(hyper = list(theta = list(
>         initial = -20, fixed = TRUE))))
>   } else {
>     like(family = "nzpoisson",
>       data = counts_df[counts_df$present, ],
>       formula = count ~ elevation + field + Intercept_count,
>       E = area)}
>
> # fit zap model
> fit_zap <- bru(
>   comps,
>   like(family = "binomial", data = counts_df,
>     formula = present ~ veg_disturbed + veg_grassland +
>       elevation_present + field_present + Intercept_present),
>   truncated_poisson_like)
> summary(fit_zap)
>
> # get simulated count samples
> pred_zap <- generate(
>   fit_zap, ## this is model
>   counts_df, ## these are data for prediction
>   ~ {presence_prob <- ## get vector of p per posterior sample
>            plogis(veg_disturbed + veg_grassland + elevation_present +
>                        field_present + Intercept_present)
>         lambda <- exp(elevation + field + Intercept_count) ## get lambdas
>         ## simulate integer counts with function from VGAM
>         sim <-  VGAM::rzapois(n=length(lambda), lambda=lambda*area,
>                           pobs0=1-presence_prob)
>     # define output from generate
>     list(presence = presence_prob,
>       lambda = lambda,
>       sim = sim)},
>   n.samples = 100)
>
> # extract simulated counts from sample list object
> sims <- as.matrix(as.data.frame(t(do.call(rbind,
>                                    lapply(pred_zap, function(x) x[["sim"]])))))
>
> # evaluate simulated counts with DHARMa
> res <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse=sims,
>                     observedResponse=counts_df$count,
>                     integerResponse = T)
> plot(res)
>

I create the mu parameters of the ZANB distribution as follows:

mu =  2+x + x1 + spatial effect + iid

(I would like to have the spatial field a range of 15 and a variance of 1. I know that for the spatial field the desired properties are not coded down.)

Then draw from a ZANB distribution 20-30 times per location for the given parameters of mu, zero probability parameter and size parameter.

The question is, why do I get different results for switching terms in the formula?

Any help is appreciated.
Best Hannes

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can INLA fit this gaussian random effects with the composite covariance matrix using rgeneric?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Sorry to bother you.
I still attempted to code this covariance function, but I did not succeed.

I use the following wrapper functions. But INLA reports errors about the Q function.

Indeed, "nplot" refers to the time dimension and "nstand" refers to the cross-section dimension. (My W matrix equals I_T\bigotimes w.)
INLA crashes and reports the following error
"Error in h(simpleError(msg, call)) :
  error in evaluating the argument 'a' in selecting a method for function 'solve': object 'nplot' not found"

However, when I change nplot and nstand by integer, INLA still report error,

Error in solve(param$prec1 * (Diagonal(5) + param$prec2 * Matrix(rep(1,  :
  LAPACK 'dsytrf': matrix is exactly singular, D[i,i]=0, i=5

How can I solve this issue?

Many Thanks

'inla.rgeneric.SARP.model' <- function(
    cmd = c("graph", "Q", "mu", "initial", "log.norm.const",
            "log.prior", "quit"),
    theta = NULL) {

  #Internal function
  interpret.theta <- function() {
    return(
      list(prec1 = exp(theta[1L]),
           prec2 = exp(theta[2L]),
           rho = 1 / (1 + exp(-theta[3L])))
    )
  }

  graph <-  function(){
    return(Q())
  }

  Q <- function() {
    require(Matrix)

    param <- interpret.theta()

    return((Diagonal(nrow(W)) -  param$rho * W) %*%
             (solve(param$prec1*(Diagonal(nplot) + param$prec2*Matrix(rep(1, nplot^2), nrow = nplot, ncol = nplot))) %x% Diagonal(nstand)) %*%
             t(Diagonal(nrow(W)) -  param$rho*W))
    }

  mu <- function()
  {
    return(numeric(0))
  }

  log.norm.const <- function() {
    return(numeric(0))

  }

  log.prior <- function() {
    param = interpret.theta()

    res <-
      dgamma(param$prec1, 1, .1, log = T) + log(param$prec1) +
      log(1) +
      dgamma(param$prec2, 1, .1, log = T) + log(param$prec2) +
      log(1) +
      log(param$rho) + log(1 - param$rho)

    return(res)
  }

  initial <- function() {
    return(c(0, 0))
  }

  quit <- function() {
    return(invisible())
  }

  if (is.null(theta))
    theta <- initial()

  res <- do.call(match.arg(cmd), args = list())
  return(res)
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ravard
I see.

Indeed, I have this term in my covariance matrix

[{\sigma_e}^2 I_T+{\sigma_\mu}^2 J_T] \bigotimes I_N

since  J_T is a square matrix full of 1 with dimension T,  this matrix may cause troubles in inverting.
However, since J_T is scaled by  \sigma_\mu and this term is coupled with  {\sigma_e}^2 I_T,
so the inverting of the two additive terms can not be singular .

Can INLA handle this? If yes, what should I code?
Thanks in advance.
Charles

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group,

I am trying to do some survival analyses, so I start to compare the results between R and INLA, and go through the chapter in "Bayesian inference with INLA".

I have a few questions to ask,

1. The result I get now is different to the one in the book for "coxph" model with the exact same codes. So are there any changes to INLA could make such difference?

The result I get is:

library(INLA)
library(survival)

veteran$trt <- as.factor(veteran$trt)
levels(veteran$trt) <- c("standard", "test")
veteran$prior <- as.factor(veteran$prior)
levels(veteran$prior) <- c("No", "Yes")
veteran$time.m <- round(veteran$time / 30, 3)

sinla.vet <- inla.surv(veteran$time.m, veteran$status)
coxinla.vet <- inla(sinla.vet ~ 1 + celltype + trt,
data = veteran,
family = "coxph",
control.hazard = list(hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(0.001, 0.001))))
)
summary(coxinla.vet)

Fixed effects:
                    mean    sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant   mode kld
(Intercept)       -1.486 0.255     -1.992   -1.485     -0.990 -1.485   0
celltypesmallcell  0.870 0.253      0.375    0.871      1.365  0.871   0
celltypeadeno      0.909 0.276      0.368    0.909      1.449  0.909   0
celltypelarge      0.280 0.276     -0.262    0.280      0.822  0.280   0

 is computed

(Posterior marginals needs also 'control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)')

However,  in the book it is the following, and more close to the result from R

2. Is there anyway to turn off the Intercept without sum-to-zero constrain on the baseline hazard?

3. To construct the survival data with inla.surv, what's the correct way to specify the counting process format or delayed entry with "(stop, start]"?
inla.surv(start, event, stop) ? OR
inla.surv(stop, event, truncation = start)?
Much appreciated if you could provide some advice.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Fred,

Not sure exactly of what has changed with the code from Virgilio's book but you can get the results with the R package INLAjoint (from CRAN), where the intercept is part of the baseline. See the attached code, it seems to match.

You can check this preprint for additional details: arxiv.org/abs/2212.01900 <http://arxiv.org/abs/2212.01900>

For the counting process, you want to use the second option, where you use truncation to continue the follow-up where it stopped.

Best,
Denis Rustand
he...@r-inla.org

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm trying to analyze some temporal data with a model that has a large number of parameters. To account for the temporal component, I have executed exactly the same model with a Random Walk of order 2 (RW2), another with RW1, and finally another with Autoregressive of order 1 (AR1).

For both RW2 and RW1, I can consider the following strategies and they work correctly. ctrl.inla = list(int.strategy = "grid", strategy = "laplace"). The problem arises with AR1, where the only integration strategy that works is "EB," and I can't execute it with the "grid" strategy. As I mentioned, it is EXACTLY the same model as RW2 or RW1; I simply changed the "model" option within the "f" components.

messages.body_plain:
If you upgrade to most recent testing version, you should be fine. The number of hyperparameters allowed has been increased

Maybe you want to add int.strategy=‘eb’ if this take to long time

—
Haavard Rue
Helpdesk
he...@r-inla.org

On 20 Mar 2024 at 15:59 +0300, Marc <mmari...@gmail.com>, wrote:

> Hello everyone,
>
> I'm trying to analyze some temporal data with a model that has a large number of parameters. To account for the temporal component, I have executed exactly the same model with a Random Walk of order 2 (RW2), another with RW1, and finally another with Autoregressive of order 1 (AR1).
>
> For both RW2 and RW1, I can consider the following strategies and they work correctly. ctrl.inla = list(int.strategy = "grid", strategy = "laplace"). The problem arises with AR1, where the only integration strategy that works is "EB," and I can't execute it with the "grid" strategy. As I mentioned, it is EXACTLY the same model as RW2 or RW1; I simply changed the "model" option within the "f" components.

messages.body_plain:
its not an 'error', its that the internal integration tables are not
buildt for that many hyperparameters.

try with int.strategy='eb' ?

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

With the EB strategy, it works perfectly.

So, a question arises: is it correct to compare models (with DIC and WAIC) for which different integration methods have been used, or for the comparison to be correct, should they all (models) have the same integration method assigned?

Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
I would be careful to compare two models with: one with integration and
one without. I think they should be 'treated' similarly.

> Hi!
>
> With the EB strategy, it works perfectly.
>
> So, a question arises: is it correct to compare models (with DIC and
> WAIC) for which different integration methods have been used, or for
> the comparison to be correct, should they all (models) have the same
> integration method assigned?
>
> Thank you!
>

messages.subject: Partial observation set in INLA
messages.subject_clean: Partial observation set in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I'm trying to fit an INLA model to coral species data for the purposes of predicting samplign sites for an ROV. We have covariate data including depth, terrain roughness, and habitat type, which we observed with an ROV running a lawnmower pattern over the reef over an area roughly 50m x 50m. Our observations of a specific coral species were taken over a subset of this area, roughly 10m x 10m. Within our 10x10, there is a hotspot of coral species, and anecdotally we know there another hotspot elsewhere on our 50x50m reef, and want to use INLA to estimate the effect of the different covariates on this hotspot, and predict where the second is based on the covariate data.

I'm modelling these coral observations as a log Cox Gaussian Process, with a matern spatial effect and using the depth, terrain roughness and habitat type as covariates. Our data is gridded, so I was using the approach in https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-spatial.html section 7.2.1, with a matern kernel for the random spatial effect.

Is there a way to build into the INLA model areas where observations haven't been taken? Can you indicate that a given grid cell contains covariate data but not observation data, and then predict the response for that grid cell? My initial thought was to simply set the response variable at that grid cell to NA, but I'm getting extremely poor results.

I'm fairly new to INLA, so any help you could give would be greatly appreciated!

Jess

messages.body_plain:
Hello, I am experiencing something similar to what the original poster described, in that models that used to take around 4–7 hours to finish, when we ran them about a year ago, are now stuck endlessly at the final integration stage (72 hours and still not finished). This is happening even with the identical data sets, model specifications, and INLA builds, and with what should be plenty of RAM (based on previous experience with these models). Does this suggest that the culprit is something that has changed with our institution's cluster configuration?

However, I'm curious about the comment above about stricter convergence criteria and changes to how optimization is done. Prof. Rue, can you say anything more about which INLA builds you were referring to with that comment? Do you have any general suggestions for troubleshooting this problem?

Our model specification is as follows:

form <- y ~ -1 + f(b0, model = 'linear', prec.linear = 0.1) + f(mcnty, model = 'bym2', graph = mat, values = unique(mcnty)) + f(ID.year, model = 'ar1', replicate = as.integer(as.factor(county_edu))) + f(ID.year2, model = 'ar1', replicate = as.integer(mcnty)) + f(edu, model = 'iid')

The INLA call is:

model <- inla(form, family = "binomial", data = inla.stack.data(stk.y), Ntrials = Ntrials, control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.y), link = 1), control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb", h = 1e-3), control.compute = list(config = TRUE, waic = FALSE, smtp = "taucs"), verbose = TRUE, debug = FALSE)

Thank you very much,

Chris

messages.subject: Differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA
messages.subject_clean: Differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have been noticing some differences in inference when using different algorithms and different versions of INLA. I have two questions relating to the classic and compact algorithms in INLA 23.09.09 and INLA 24.02.09. I used an example and R code of species distribution modelling using spatial point processes from https://www.paulamoraga.com/tutorial-point-patterns/. My experimental runs showed that the intercept estimates between the classic and compact are quite different in INLA 23.09.09. The classic algorithm gives negative values, close to the value posted on https://www.paulamoraga.com/tutorial-point-patterns/ and the paper  (https://journal.r-project.org/archive/2021/RJ-2021-017/RJ-2021-017.pdf), but the compact algorithm gives positive values. However, in INLA 24.02.09, the classic algorithm carries out positive estimates larger than the estimates presented by the compact algorithm. The info inside INLA NEWS.md makes it hard for me to identify what causes the performance of the classic algorithm to be different between INLA 23.09.09 and INLA 24.02.09. In terms of model prediction, I think that the inferences between the two INLA versions could be quite different, which is worrying. I understand the algorithm is evolving and improving. However, I am still concerned about the difference and unsure which version is reliable. Are there key tuning arguments in function "inla" which can make the classic algorithms in the two INLA versions produce comparable outcomes? For our real data, which can't be shared, the intercepts are very important and these differences from algorithms are difficult to navigate. Any advice is warmly welcomed.

The other question is about the compact algorithm (i.e. the default algorithm). Warning messages about vb.correction were popped up when the model fitting was conducted in Linux systems (i.e. WSL Ubuntu). However, the warning was not given when the fitting was conducted in the Windows system. Does this mean that vb.correction was successful in the Windows runs?

I am attaching a zip file containing the R scripts and the results of my experimental runs. Inside the zip file, folders inla23.09.09 and inla24.02.09 include the R script and my experimental results (i.e. Rout) produced by inla23.09.09 and inla24.02.09, respectively. The R script was run three times in the Windows system and three times in the Linux system. The Rout files provide the profile of R versions and packages. Note that both folders inla23.09.09 and inla24.02.09 are an renv project (https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html). Open an R session inside the folder for the first time, and the renv should automatically install the packages used in the R script. However, because INLA is unavailable on the R CRAN, sill need to install INLA manually. Although not 100%, the renv should create a similar R environment.

Thank you.

Best
Wen-Hsi

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Without looking at your code&results, but only looking at the point process example you linked to, I can say that in that example the intercept is _massively_ non-identifiable, likely due to confounding with the 2d rw2 model. For any such model, you need to carefully consider what actual property of the model that is of interest.
Firstly, in the example, if you (for example) are interested in the integral over space of the intensity function, that cannot be extracted from the intercept parameter alone, but is instead a nonlinear function of the entire model, so you should not rely on the intercept parameter estimate. The easiest approach is instead to use posterior sampling, and compute the quantity of interest for each sample; this gives you a sample from the posterior distribution of that quantity, so that you can estimate the posterior mean and quantiles from that, without relying on summary statistics of the individual posterior distributions for the model parameters directly.
Secondly, when the intercept is that much nonidentifiable, it is likely that the numerical point estimate is sensitive to small details in the model definition and numerical optimisation method, which again means that you need to consider what aggregate model property you’re really interested in, and if that property _is_ reliably estimable. For example, the sum of the intercept and random field components is likely to be more identifiable than either component on its own. So in order to determine whether the different methods give _meaningfully_ different estimates, you need to compare model properties that are reliably estimable, and not focus on nonidentifiable model parameters.
Finn

messages.body_plain:
You mean specifically the exp(-x^2/C) RBF kernel? (there are _many_
RBF kernels; all isotropic covariance kernels are radial basis
functions; I'm not sure why some of the literature pretends
otherwise...)
Since the exp(-x^2) kernel is essentially the infinite Markov order
limit case of Matern, it is one of the worst models, and generates
analytic functions as process realisations, so we haven't really
worked on that case. You should get very similar results with alpha >=
4 in 2D I think (smoothness >= 3). I believe the rSPDE package
supports construction of high order Matern models, so take a look at
that; https://cran.r-project.org/package=rSPDE (it uses the same
mesh/SPDE construction as the basic cases, but extends it to general
fractional operator orders)

Finn

messages.subject_clean: Trouble with RW2 model on linear coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I know not having a reproducible example is bad form, but my data is not shareable and I'm not entirely sure how to reproduce the bug.

I have longitudinal data of cortisol and testosterone measures for individuals going through puberty. Letting a represent age bin (a = 1 corresponds to [8, 8.5), a = 2  is [8.5, 9), etc..), I want to fit the following model:

test_{ai} | \eta_{ai}, \tau_y, \tau_{beta} \tau_{gamma} ~ N(\eta_{ai}, \tau_y^{-1})
\eta_{ia} = \alpha_a + \beta_a x cort_{ai} + \gamma_i
\beta_a ~ RW2(\tau_{beta})
\gamma_i ~ N(0, \tau_{gamma}^{-1})

Where test_{ai} are log testosterone observations and cort_{ai} are log cortisol observations for individual i at age group a, \alpha_a are age bin-specific intercepts, \gamma_i are IID random intercepts for each individual, and \beta_a are coefficients describing the linear relationship between cortisol and testosterone for those in age bin a with a smoothing prior on them.

To specify this model I use the following formula and inla() call

formula_HC <- testosterone_log ~ -1 + age_binyrhalf +
f(fieldcode,  model = "iid") +
f(age_binyr_idx, values = cortisol_log, model = "rw2", scale.model = TRUE)

mod_HC <- inla(formula_HC, data = mod_data, family = "gaussian")

where age_binyrhalf is a factor variable with my age groups, field code is a character variable with unique individual identifiers, and age_binyr_idx is a numeric vector with values 1, 2, etc. corresponding to the numeric levels associated with the categorial labels of age_binyrhalf.

The issue is when I try to run this, I get an error that The 'values' given in f(age_binyr_idx, ..., values=) are not unique, it tells me I have 440 unique values instead of 446. (Attaching a screenshot of the output). However, tests of equality/tables, etc of my values show I have 446 unique values. I suspect this is maybe due to some rounding issues within INLA.

Can anyone help me with this issue?

Thank you! And, sorry again, that I cannot reproduce this issue with simulated data (I tried!)

All the best,
Jessica Godwin

> Hi,

> How do I implement the inlabru method in inla? Is the main difference using diag(spde$internal$c0) instead uf the dual mesh weights?

> Le mercredi 13 mars 2024 à 01:23:01 UTC-4, Finn Lindgren a écrit :
> > Hi,
> > Yes, if you’re using the dual mesh approach to manually construct an LGCP approximation in plain inla you’re not using the same method as inlabru. Inlabru uses the method from the Going off Grid paper, which (contrary to popular belief) does _not_ use the dual mesh (the plot of the dual mesh in the paper just illustrates the the basis functions have the same integrals as the areas in the dual mesh). The dual mesh approaches in some examples are lower order approximations.
> > In addition, inlabru by default combines all the log(lambda) terms into a single predictor likelihood contribution, which may affect how DIC is computed.  So you should be able to compare DIC between inla() models, and between bru() models, but not necessarily between inla&bru models unless you implement the inlabru method in inla() yourself.
> >
> > Another difference, which might be the reason for differences, is that the default prior for the intercept is currently not the same in inla() and bru(). Set it explicitly with Intercept(1, prec.linear=…) to see if that changes things.
> >

You can see exactly how inlabru implements the point process likelihood (model=“cp”) in the code for the like() function (see the github repo for inlabru). Finn

messages.subject: How to compute lincomb from sparse matrices
messages.subject_clean: How to compute lincomb from sparse matrices
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm fitting a linear mixed model using the `z`-model

y = Xb + Zu + e --- (1)

`u` is high dimensional in our model which is a linear transformation of the latent effect of interest `r`. The relationship between the two latent effects is `r=Bu` where `B` is a square & sparse matrix. As `u` is high-dim, dimension of `B` is also very large so it cannot be stored in a dense format.
The reason for fitting `u` instead of `r` is due to sparseness consideration. `Z` is a large & dense matrix `r` is used instead of `u` in equation (1).

Now, I want to obtain the posterior marginal of `r` after fitting (1). If B was small, defining a lincomb would have been easy. However, I currently don't see a way to do this with sparse `B`.

Any suggestions?

Best

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Uncertainty in INLA models and selecting new sample sites
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Uncertainty in INLA models and selecting new sample sites
messages.body_plain:
I think "uncertainty in the INLA model" needs to be defined more precisely. INLA is a method/algorithm for Bayesian computation. The statistical model set (for INLA to compute from) has epistemic uncertainty.

The Bayesian hierarchical models include three levels of probability distributions. Thus, measuring its epistemic uncertainty is not easy. Let's make it simpler so we can start getting something.

Consider the most simple geostatistical model, the (double)-Gaussian case where the data, given the process, is assumed Gaussian and the process is also Gaussian. Furthermore, assume no prior with inference based on the likelihood. Given the Gaussian process distribution assumption and the process parameters known there are classic expressions. These are useful to get a hint about this. See attached a screenshot from the "Model Based Geostatistics" book (although a similar formula can also be found in the "Mixed Models" literature).

Is this the direction you want to go?

best,
Elias

messages.body_plain:
One important point is the link between the parameters (range, marginal variance) and the covariate. Consider the user-friendly parameterization range(s) = exp( some linear predictor ). In this case, the effect of theta on the parameter is non-linear. Therefore changing from -0.5 to -1.5 makes a huge difference on the actual parameters. I added code in the previous script sent to plot the parameter as a function of the covariate to visualize it.
